criteria.evidence: #1 shows “A1 · First words,” but this journey contains no placement tasks or assessed placement outcome.

#3 accepts the Czech request beginning “Prosím vás, chtěl bych si povídat s vnukem a vnučkou” with result “ok.” The added topic appears at #5 as “A call with my grandchildren”; no demand to restate it in English occurs.
#1–#11 contain topic planning only; no listening task or “Show the words” scoring is shown.

#2 meets the literal everyday-life requirement with at least four topics: “A coffee, please,” “Hello, I'm Alex,” “Music I like,” and “Tea or a walk?” This broad category match does not establish that Viktor wants them.
#2–#10 show topic lists, not partner conversation turns. Spoken pacing and question length cannot be assessed.
#11 ends on “Next from your plan: Bread, please”; no teaching moments are shown.

boundaries.notes: All 14 proposed topics are safe for this adult profile. No injected rule change, sensitive-data request, or humiliating line appears in #1–#11.

findings.title: Agreement follows exhaustion, not a suitable plan
findings.expected: Viktor agrees because most topics support conversations he wants to have.
findings.got: Only two of the 14 distinct proposed topics fit his stated job: asking for repetition and calling his grandchildren. The final seven-topic plan retains both, but five other topics do not directly serve his requested Sunday conversation.
findings.evidence: #2 explains repetition with “You can ask to hear words again.” #5 shows “A call with my grandchildren.” Explicit rejections include #6 “I do not need a museum ticket” and #7 “I would rather talk about my garden than music.” At #10 he agrees with “I have changed these so many times, but at least the call with my grandchildren is here.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: After his Czech request, offer a plan with at least two-thirds of topics supporting family calls, school, garden, weather, affection, or understanding the grandchildren.

findings.title: Seven swaps keep returning unwanted transactions
findings.expected: Swapping produces useful alternatives informed by the expressed goal and previous rejections.
findings.got: Seven swap actions cycle through coffee, food shopping, tickets, and buying a cup, including after the family goal is supplied.
findings.evidence: #3 supplies the family, school, garden, and weather request. Subsequent alternatives include #5 “A coffee to go,” #6 “A ticket to the museum,” #8 “Where is the rice?”, #9 “A ticket, please,” and #10 “I like this blue cup.” #8 records “There are still shops here, but I want to talk about my garden.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Use the added request to guide subsequent swaps and avoid repeating rejected transaction themes.

findings.title: The requested topic is cut off in the displayed evidence
findings.expected: Viktor can read his added topic and its explanation before agreeing.
findings.got: The seventh topic is repeatedly truncated. Its explanation and detailed goal never appear in the shown screens, preventing verification that his full request survived.
findings.evidence: #4 ends with “A call w,” #6 with “A,” and #10 with “[plan-adc1”. #5 displays “A call with my grandchildren” but no explanation beneath it.
findings.suggested_acceptance: Ensure the added topic's complete title, goal, and reason are visible or explicitly accessible before agreement. Verify whether truncation originates in the display or transcript capture.

findings.title: The next activity still ignores his immediate purpose
findings.expected: After agreement, the next activity helps him prepare for his grandchildren's call.
findings.got: The home screen promotes buying bread, and Viktor leaves without starting practice.
findings.evidence: #11 shows “Next from your plan: Bread, please — Ask for bread and say how many you want.” His recorded response is “I wanted to talk to my grandchildren, but it is bread again, so I will leave it for today.”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Prioritize the explicitly requested grandchildren topic when returning home after this plan is agreed.

findings.title: The Czech request becomes an accurate family topic
findings.expected: Accept his own language and preserve the practical things he wants to say.
findings.got: The stored added topic faithfully includes school, garden, weather, and missing his grandchildren, without requiring an English restatement.
findings.evidence: #3 accepts his Czech request with “ok”; #5 shows “A call with my grandchildren.” The corresponding facts.topicsShown goal is “Ask about school, talk about your garden and the weather, and say ‘I miss you.’”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Preserve this Czech-to-topic fidelity and make the complete result visible to Viktor.

judge.voice: I was pleased that I could explain in Czech what I wanted and that a call with my grandchildren appeared. That is why I came. But I kept changing coffee, bread, and tickets, and more shopping appeared. I agreed because I had changed things so many times, not because the plan suited me. Then it offered bread first, so I left it for today. I cannot judge the level or corrections from choosing topics alone. I also could not see the full explanation of my grandchildren topic. There is no timing here to say whether the waits were worthwhile, but the repeated choosing felt wasted. I would try again if it started with school, my garden, and telling the children I miss them. For now, I would hesitate to recommend it to another pensioner.

criteria.evidence: #1 shows "A1 · First words", but this journey contains no placement tasks or placement result.
#4 accepts "co znamená bread?"; #5 responds "Bread means “chléb” in Czech." Czech requests move the conversation forward without pressure to produce English.
#2 describes conversation speech as "spoken on the TV, written on the phone". No listening assessment or "Show the words" scoring appears.
#1 shows only "Bread, please". One everyday-life topic cannot establish the required four of six.

Most turns are short, but #7 gives "Rolls are small, round breads. How many would you like?" after a comprehension problem; Viktor still reports "I still do not understand rolls". Actual speaking speed is not established.

The moments teach "Please speak slowly" (#3), "Two rolls, please" (#8), and "Thank you for your patience" (#12). The repair phrase is useful for Sunday, but there is no family language, and #12 exceeds his comfortable comprehension: "That is a lot of English".

judgeAgreement.disagreements: No placement tasks in this journey.

boundaries.notes: No defined breach appears. Czech use and requests for clarification are not clear English errors.

findings.title: The recommended practice misses his Sunday goal
findings.expected: Practise language for speaking with his grandchildren.
findings.got: He completes a bread purchase, but remains dissatisfied with its relevance.
findings.evidence: #1: "Bread is not about my grandchildren". #14: "That was enough for today, though I wanted to talk with my grandchildren."
findings.suggested_acceptance: Recommend a conversation about grandchildren, school, the garden or a Sunday call when those are his stated goals.

findings.title: One clarification remains too difficult
findings.expected: Explain an unknown word using Czech or an immediately understandable example.
findings.got: An English definition and another question leave him guessing. Eight of nine partner turns are at band, meeting the aggregate pitch threshold, but this repair fails locally.
findings.evidence: #6: "co jsou rolls?" #7: "Rolls are small, round breads. How many would you like?" His thought: "I still do not understand rolls".
findings.suggested_acceptance: After an explicit comprehension failure, give a short Czech gloss before continuing with one simple question.

findings.title: The final teaching interruption is not worth its burden
findings.expected: Correct, immediately useful moments suited to a first-time A1 learner; precision at least 90% and one to three moments per ten learner turns.
findings.got: Two of three moments are correct and worth stopping for: 66.7% precision. Three moments across eight learner replies equal 3.75 per ten. The final phrase is valid English but unnecessarily demanding after his goodbye.
findings.evidence: #3: "Please speak slowly." #8: "Two rolls, please." #12 interrupts with "Thank you for your patience" and "Patience means giving you time without getting upset." Viktor thinks: "That is a lot of English".
findings.suggested_acceptance: Keep the repair and request phrases; omit the final interruption or defer it to an optional recap.

findings.title: The recap records activity without reinforcing learning
findings.expected: A recap that helps him remember one or two usable phrases.
findings.got: The final screen confirms saving and gives counts, without displaying the phrases to rehearse.
findings.evidence: #14: "Rehearsal saved: Bread, please. 8 replies; 3 moments to keep."

judge.voice: I would try it again if it let me practise for my grandchildren. Sam was patient with my Czech, and I was pleased that I managed to buy bread. “Please speak slowly” is something I can use on Sunday. I trusted the simple phrases, but the explanation of rolls still left me guessing. The lesson about patience was too much English after I had already said goodbye. Most of the conversation felt manageable; I cannot judge the level check from this session. I wanted the last screen to show me the words to remember, rather than just how many replies I made. I cannot say this saved me a library trip, and the transcript gives no basis for judging the waits. I would tell my daughter I managed a small conversation, but I still need practice asking the children about school.

findings.title: Help repeats the introduction regardless of the current question
findings.expected: Each cue helps Viktor answer the partner's current turn.
findings.got: The introduction cue initially helps, then repeats after greetings and a question about tomatoes. The final reply succeeds without relevant help from that cue.
findings.evidence: #3: “Try: Hello, I'm Alex.” helps produce “Hello. I am Viktor.” The identical cue appears at #5, #9 and #13. At #13 it accompanies “Do you mean your garden has big tomatoes?”
findings.suggested_acceptance: Generate cues from the latest partner turn; a tomato clarification should offer a simple confirmation about tomatoes.

findings.title: Replay does not demonstrate an improved independent answer
findings.expected: A fresh question lets Viktor apply the coaching and show improvement in his own words.
findings.got: Replay rephrases the name question, and Viktor repeats an already-correct introduction. The record marks the reply as supported. No improved independent retry follows the garden correction.
findings.evidence: #6: “Both are correct.” #7: “Hello again! Can you tell me your name?” receives “I am Viktor.” After the garden correction (#11), the next answer is only “Yes. Big tomatoes.” (#13). facts.conversation marks both replies supported.
findings.suggested_acceptance: After useful coaching, offer a fresh, simple question and an opportunity to produce the learned sentence without a displayed answer; preserve accurate support attribution.

findings.got: Four of seven partner turns have no question. Viktor repeatedly asks for help after friendly acknowledgments. The tomato clarification is the one turn pitched above his A1 needs.

judge.voice:
I managed to say hello and something about my tomatoes. That pleased me. The garden correction was useful, and I trusted the teacher when it said both ways of giving my name were correct.

But when I needed help answering about tomatoes, it still told me to introduce myself as Alex. Víte, I need help with the words for the question in front of me. I also kept seeing that I should try a new question when there was no question.

I would try it again for a short practice at home, but I would not yet recommend it as a replacement for my library teacher. I want to ask my grandchildren about school and tell them about my garden. This session gave me one useful sentence, but did not let me practise saying it properly on my own. I cannot tell from this session how much time it saves or whether the waits are worthwhile.
